For those saying there's no chance it happens, or doesn't happen without armed conflict, while I agree it's incredibly unlikely, I don't think it's impossible. For one thing, there are statehood movements in liberal strongholds of Washington DC and Puerto Rico.

Politically speaking, the move would cut the state's population roughly in half, and therefore would split the number of house reps about equally, and create two new senate seats. California has 53 members of the house, and like every state, 2 senators. Currently the California house delegation is split 40/13 Ds to Rs. The districts are gerrymandered a little bit to give the democrats an advantage, but Ds would almost certainly still carry some seats in urban San Diego, and they really wouldn't lose a single one in Old California. At most, this move causes the Republicans to gain 13 seats in the house of representatives. As for the Senate, well, Old California would elect two blue senators as they do already and New California would elect two red senators almost certainly. So the secession alone would add 13 Red seats to the house and 2 Red senators. This would also cause New and Old California to split their Electoral votes, with about 29 remaining blue for Old California and 28 now going red for New California.

When you look at the Rs picking up 13 house seats, 2 Senators and 28 electoral votes, it doesn't seem very likely that this will ever happen.

However, Washington DC and Puerto Rico then enter the picture.

Both would get 2 senators, all 4 would be blue, along with one rep for DC and 4 or 5 for Puerto Rico, also solid blue. It would also be 6 or 7 electoral votes (DC already gets 3 despite not being a state), again, all blue.

So if you admit all three as states, Republicans would only net about 8 Reps and 21 electoral votes, and the Dems would come out ahead 2 senators. This is also assuming that New California would be as solidly red as DC and PR would be solidly blue, which seems unlikely, as the Dems could probably pick up some house seats in New California, and even a senator every once in awhile (they've done it in Indiana, Alabama, etc.) while the Republicans would virtually never pick off a rep in Old California, DC or PR, as they would be literally the bluest states in the country.

So the tradeoff would be something like 6-8 reps and 21 electoral votes in exchange for 2 senators. That's about as even of a trade as you can make considering that the margin of control of the house is usually more than 6-8 seats and the electoral college usually more than 21 votes, while the Senate will often swing much closer. It's hard to quantify exactly how much more valuable a senate seat is than a house seat or an electoral vote, but somewhere between 4 and 10X seems right, even if that is a wide margin. When you consider that the deal could net 3 senators for the Dems, and possibly even cost them no electoral votes every once in a while, the deal starts to make even more sense.
